knowledgePattern: Audit whether squaring a radical inequality is reversible on its domain
solution:
The square root requires x≥3. On this domain, x−2≥1, so both sides are nonnegative and squaring preserves the strict inequality in both directions.

The squared inequality is x−3<(x−2)2, equivalent to x2−5x+7>0. Its discriminant is 25−28=−3, and its leading coefficient is positive, so it is positive for every real input.

Equivalently, x2−5x+7=(x−5/2)2+3/4>0. Hence every x≥3 works, including x=3, where 0<1. Every displayed step is valid. Answer G.

hints.title: Check the signs before squaring
hints.body: First use the square-root domain to decide the sign of x−2. Is squaring reversible on that domain?
hints.recap: A squared equation or inequality must retain the original sign and domain restrictions.
hints.pitfall: Squaring is not generally order-preserving when negative values are allowed.
hints.pause: Audit the first transformation using those signs.

recall.reminder: A squared equation or inequality must retain the original sign and domain restrictions.

hints.title: Check the quadratic conclusion
hints.body: Recalculate the expanded quadratic and its discriminant, or complete its square. Then compare its solution set with the original domain.
hints.recap: The leading coefficient and discriminant together determine whether a quadratic is strictly positive everywhere.
hints.pitfall: A negative discriminant alone does not identify the sign without the leading coefficient.
hints.pause: Verify the remaining proof lines, including the domain endpoint.

recall.reminder: The leading coefficient and discriminant together determine whether a quadratic is strictly positive everywhere.
